t.6.66.1: Seeing Makarākṣa come forth, those bulls among the monkeys all leapt up at once and stood ready, eager to fight.
t.6.66.2: Then there began that very great, hair-raising battle of the monkeys with the night-rangers, like that of the gods with the Dānavas.
t.6.66.3: Then the monkeys and the night-rangers crushed one another with the falling blows of trees and spears, and with the hurling down of rocks and iron clubs.
t.6.66.4: On every side the night-rangers struck with spears, pikes, maces and swords, with lances, with paṭṭisas and bhindipālas, and with volleys of arrows.
t.6.66.5: With nooses, mallets and staves, and likewise with crushing blows and other weapons, those night-rangers wrought slaughter among the lion-like monkeys.
t.6.66.6: Tormented by the floods of arrows from the son of Khara, all the Vānaras, their minds bewildered and stricken with fear, fled away.
t.6.66.7: Seeing those forest-dwellers fleeing, all the rākṣasas, thrilled and flushed with victory, roared like lions.
t.6.66.8: Then, as those monkeys were fleeing in all directions, Rāma held back those rākṣasas with a shower of arrows.
t.6.66.9: Seeing the rākṣasas held back, the night-roaming Makarākṣa, consumed by the fire of his anger, spoke these words.
t.6.66.10: Stand, Rāma! I grant you single combat with me. With sharp arrows loosed from my bow I shall make you give up your life.
t.6.66.11: Remembering how you once slew my father in the Daṇḍaka forest, before my very eyes, while he stood engaged in his own duty, my wrath swells ever greater.
t.6.66.12: My limbs burn fiercely, O wicked Rāghava, because you were not seen by me at that time in the great forest.
t.6.66.14: Today, having gone to the realm of the king of the dead by the force of my arrows, you will be united with those heroes who were slain by you.
t.6.66.13: By good fortune, Rāma, you have come here within my sight. You have been longed for, as an ordinary beast is longed for by a lion tormented with hunger.
t.6.66.15: What use is there in saying much here? Hear my words, Rāma: let all the worlds behold you and me on the field of battle.
t.6.66.16: Whether with missiles, with a mace, or with his two arms in the great battle, O Rāma, let each one fight in combat with whatever he has practiced.
t.6.66.17: Hearing the words of Makarākṣa, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, laughed and spoke these words to him who kept answering back with ever more boastful speech.
t.6.66.18: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas, and the one who was your father, as well as Triśirā and Dūṣaṇa, were slain by me in the Daṇḍaka forest.
t.6.66.19: Today indeed, O sinful one, vultures, jackals and crows, their sharp beaks and claws like goads, will be well sated with your flesh.
t.6.66.20: Thus addressed by Rāma, the night-roaming son of Khara released floods of arrows at that Rāghava on the field of battle.
t.6.66.21: With a shower of arrows Rāma cut those arrows into many pieces; severed, those gold-feathered shafts fell to the ground by the thousands.
t.6.66.22: Then there took place a battle, as they met each other with might, between the son of the rākṣasa Khara and the son of Daśaratha.
t.6.66.23: Then, on the battlefield, a sound is heard where bowstring strikes palm-guard, like the roar of two thunderclouds in the sky, a sound loosed from the bow and surpassing all in its loudness.
t.6.66.24: The Devas, Dānavas and Gandharvas, the Kiṃnaras and the great Uragas, all stationed in the sky, were eager to behold that wondrous sight.
t.6.66.26: In the battle the Rākṣasa cut down the floods of arrows loosed by Rāma, and Rāma in turn, with his own arrows, cut to pieces in many ways those loosed by the Rākṣasa.
t.6.66.25: Pierced in each other's limbs, their strength grows twofold; on the battlefield the two trade blow for blow against each other.
t.6.66.27: All the cardinal directions, and likewise the intermediate directions, were overspread with floods of arrows; and the earth too, covered on every side, could no longer be seen.
t.6.66.28: Then the mighty-armed one, enraged, cut through the bow of the rākṣasa, and Rāghava next pierced his charioteer with eight iron arrows. Shattering the chariot with his arrows, Rāma struck down the chariot's horses.
t.6.66.29: Deprived of his chariot, the night-roamer Makarākṣa stood upon the earth; standing on the earth, the rākṣasa seized in his hand a spear that struck terror into all beings and blazed like the fire at the end of the age.
t.6.66.30: And that night-roamer, whirling his great blazing spear, hurled it in fury at Rāghava in the great battle.
t.6.66.31: But Rāghava, with three arrows, cut down in mid-air that blazing spear as it came hurtling toward him, hurled from the hand of Khara's son.
t.6.66.32: That spear, adorned with heavenly gold, cut into many pieces and smitten by Rāma's arrows, shattered and fell upon the earth like a great meteor.
t.6.66.33: Seeing that spear struck down by Rāma of wondrous deeds, the beings stationed in the sky cried out, "Well done! Well done!"
t.6.66.34: Seeing that spear struck down, the night-roaming Makarākṣa raised his fist and said to Kākutstha, "Stand, stand!"
t.6.66.35: Seeing it falling toward him, Rāma, the delight of the Raghus, laughed, and then fitted the fire-missile to his own bow.
t.6.66.36: Struck then in battle by Kākutstha with that missile, the demon, its heart split apart, fell there and died.
t.6.66.37: Seeing the fall of Makarākṣa, all those Rākṣasas, tormented by Rāma's arrows, then fled back to Laṅkā itself.
t.6.66.38: Then the gods, overjoyed, beheld that night-roaming son of Khara slain by the swift force of the arrows of King Daśaratha's son, lying shattered like a mountain struck down by the thunderbolt.
